source_text: Μὴ παραλογίσηταί σέ τις τῷ πολυσήμῳ τῆς λέξεως. Πολλαὶ γὰρ ἀρχαὶ πολλῶν πραγμάτων κατὰ τὸν βίον τοῦτον· ἀλλὰ μία ἀρχὴ ἐπὶ πάντων, ἡ ἐπέκεινα. Ἀρχὴ γὰρ ὁδοῦ ἀγαθῆς, εἶπεν ἡ Παροιμία. Ἀλλ' ὁδοῦ μὲν ἀρχὴ ἡ πρώτη κίνησις, ὅθεν ἀρχόμεθα τῆς πορείας, ἧς τὸ κατόπιν δυνατόν ἐστιν εὑρεῖν. Καὶ, Ἀρχὴ σοφίας φόβος Κυρίου. Ἔστι καὶ ταύτης τῆς ἀρχῆς ἕτερόν τι προκείμενον· τῆς γὰρ τῶν τεχνῶν ἀναλήψεως ἀρχή ἐστιν ἡ στοιχείωσις. Στοιχεῖον οὖν ἐστι τῆς σοφίας ὁ φόβος τοῦ Κυρίου· ἀλλὰ ταύτης τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐστί τι πρεσβύτερον, ἡ κατάστασις τῆς ψυχῆς, τοῦ μήπω σοφισθέντος καὶ τὸν φόβον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀνειληφότος. Ἀρχαὶ λέ γονται καὶ αἱ πολιτικαὶ δυναστεῖαι, αἱ τῶν ἀξιωμά των ὑπεροχαί. Ἀλλ' αὗται αἱ ἀρχαὶ, τινῶν εἰσιν ἀρχαὶ, καὶ πρός τι ἑκάστη . Ἀρχὴ γὰρ τῆς γραμμῆς τὸ σημεῖον· καὶ ἀρχὴ τῆς ἐπιφανείας ἡ γραμμή· καὶ ἀρχὴ τοῦ σώματος ἡ ἐπιφάνεια· καὶ τοῦ κατὰ σύνθεσιν λόγου ἀρχαὶ τὰ στοιχεῖα. Οὐ μὴν κἀκείνη τοιαύτη ἡ ἀρχή. Οὐδενὶ γὰρ προσδέδεται· οὐδενὶ δουλεύει· μετ' οὐδενὸς θεωρεῖ ται· ἀλλ' ἐλευθέρα ἐστίν· ἀδέσποτος, λελυμένη τῆς πρὸς ἕτερον σχέσεως· ἀνυπέρβατος διανοίᾳ, ἣν οὐκ ἔστιν ὑπερβῆναι τοῖς λογισμοῖς, ἧς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐξευρεῖν τὰ ἐπέκεινα. Ἐὰν γὰρ φιλονεικήσῃς τῇ φαντασίᾳ τοῦ νοῦ παραδραμεῖν τὴν ἀρχὴν, εὑρήσεις αὐτὴν προτρέχουσάν σου, καὶ προαπαντῶσαν τοῖς λογισμοῖς. Ἄφες σεαυτοῦ τὸν νοῦν δραμεῖν ὅσον βού λεται, καὶ διαταθῆναι ἐπὶ τὰ ἄνω· εἶτα εὑρήσεις αὐτὸν μυρία πλανηθέντα, καὶ πολλὰ κενεμβατήσαντα, καὶ πάλιν ἐπανιόντα πρὸς ἑαυτὸν, διὰ τὸ μὴ δύνα σθαι κατωτέραν ἑαυτοῦ τὴν ἀρχὴν ποιῆσαι. Διότι ἀεὶ τοῦ νοουμένου ἐξωτέρα καὶ πλείων εὑρίσκεται ἡ ἀρχή. Ἐν ἀρχῇ τοίνυν ἦν ὁ Λόγος. Ὢ τοῦ θαύματος! Πῶς πᾶσαι ἀλλήλαις ὁμοτίμως αἱ φωναὶ συνεζεύχθησαν! Τὸ, Ἦν, ἴσον δύναται τοῦ, Ἐν ἀρχῇ. Ποῦ ὁ βλάσφημος; ποῦ ἡ χριστομάχος γλῶττα; ἡ λέγουσα, Ἦν ποτε, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν; Ἄκουε τοῦ Εὐαγ-γελίου, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν. Εἰ δὲ ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν, πότε οὐκ ἦν; Τὴν ἀσέβειαν αὐτῶν στενάξω, ἢ τὴν ἀμα θίαν βδελύξομαι; Ἀλλὰ πρὸ τοῦ γεννηθῆναι, οὐκ ἦν. Οἶδας γὰρ πότε ἐγεννήθη, ἵνα τὸ πρὶν δυνηθῇς ἐπ ενεγκεῖν τῷ χρόνῳ; Τὸ γὰρ, Πρὸ τοῦ, χρονική ἐστι φωνὴ, ἕτερον ἑτέρου προτιθεῖσα εἰς παλαιότητα. Τὸν δὲ τοῦ χρόνου ποιητὴν πῶς εὔλογον ταῖς χρονικαῖς προσηγορίαις ὑποκειμένην ἔχειν τὴν γέννησιν; Ἐν ἀρχῇ τοίνυν ἦν. Ἐὰν μὴ ἀποστῇς τοῦ Ἦν, οὐδεμίαν παρείσδυσιν δώσεις τῇ πονηρᾷ βλασφημίᾳ. Ὥσπερ γὰρ οἱ θαλαττεύοντες, ὅταν ἐπὶ δύο σαλεύωσιν ἀγκυρῶν, καταφρονοῦσι τοῦ κλύδωνος· οὕτω καὶ σὺ τῆς πονηρᾶς ταύτης ταραχῆς, τῆς ἐκ τῶν πνευμάτων τῆς πονηρίας ἐγγινομένης τῷ βίῳ, καὶ διασαλευούσης τῶν πολλῶν τὴν πίστιν, καταγελάσῃ, ἐὰν τῇ ἀσφαλείᾳ τῶν ῥημάτων τούτων τὴν ψυχὴν ἔχῃς ἐνορμισθεῖσαν. Ἐπιζητεῖ δὲ ἡμῶν ἡ διάνοια, τίς ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ; Ὁ Λόγος, φησί. Ποῖος λόγος; ὁ ἀνθρώπινος λόγος; ἀλλ' ὁ τῶν ἀγγέλων λόγος; Καὶ γὰρ ᾐνίξατο ἡμῖν ὁ Ἀπόστολος, ὡς καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων ἰδίαν ἐχόντων γλῶσσαν, εἰπών· Ἐὰν ταῖς γλώσσαις τῶν ἀνθρώ πων λαλῶ καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων.
thought_title: The one beginning beyond all others
orientation: Basil is answering the objection that “beginning” is an ordinary word by distinguishing the many beginnings of this life from the one beginning that is beyond everything.
pass_a_gloss: Let no one deceive you by the many meanings of the word. For there are many beginnings of many things in this life; but there is one beginning over all things, the one beyond. For “beginning of a good way,” Proverbs said. But of a way the beginning is the first movement, from which we begin the journey, of which it is possible to find what lies behind. And, “Beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord.” There is also something else set before this beginning; for of the taking up of the arts the beginning is the elementary instruction. An element therefore of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; but of this beginning there is something older, the settled state of the soul, of the one not yet made wise and having taken up the fear of God. Beginnings are also called the political powers, the pre-eminences of offices. But these beginnings are beginnings of certain things, and each is relative to something. For beginning of the line is the point; and beginning of the surface is the line; and beginning of the body is the surface; and of the word according to composition the beginnings are the elements. But that beginning is not such. For it is bound to nothing; it serves nothing; it is contemplated with nothing; but it is free; without a master, released from relation to another; not to be passed beyond by thought, which it is not possible to pass beyond by reasonings, of which it is not possible to find out what lies beyond. For if you strive with the imagination of the mind to run past the beginning, you will find it running ahead of you, and meeting your reasonings beforehand. Let your mind run as far as it wishes, and stretch itself to the things above; then you will find it having wandered ten thousand ways, and having stepped much on emptiness, and again returning to itself, because it is not able to make the beginning lower than itself. Because always the beginning is found to be outside and greater than what is thought. In the beginning therefore was the Word. O the wonder! How all the sounds were joined together with equal honor to one another! The “was” has equal force with the “in the beginning.” Where is the blasphemer? Where is the Christ-fighting tongue? The one saying, “There was once when he was not”? Hear the Gospel: “In the beginning he was.” But if he was in the beginning, when was he not? Shall I groan at their impiety, or shall I loathe their ignorance? “But before he was begotten, he was not.” For do you know when he was begotten, so that you can attach the “before” to the time? For the “before” is a temporal expression, setting one thing before another in antiquity. But how is it reasonable that the generation of the maker of time should be subject to temporal names? In the beginning therefore he was. If you do not let go of the “was,” you will give no entrance to the wicked blasphemy. For just as sailors, when they ride on two anchors, despise the swell; so also you will laugh at this wicked disturbance, the one coming into life from the spirits of wickedness and shaking the faith of the many, if you have your soul anchored in the safety of these words. And our mind seeks: who was in the beginning? The Word, it says. What sort of word? The human word? But the word of angels? For indeed the Apostle hinted to us that angels also have their own tongue, saying: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels.”

choices.why: Keeps the spatial metaphor of the Greek, which Basil uses to stress that this beginning cannot be passed or left behind.

choices.english: not to be passed beyond by thought
choices.why: Preserves the dative of respect and the verbal idea of passing beyond, which is central to Basil's argument.
rejected: beyond the reach of the mind

choices.why: Renders the vivid compound literally to show the mind's futile wandering.
Keeps the compound's force and Basil's polemical tone.
The noun suggests creeping in sideways; 'entrance' keeps the spatial idea without over-translating.
Continues the nautical metaphor Basil introduces with the sailors and anchors.

bible_refs.note: Ἐὰν ταῖς γλώσσαις τῶν ἀνθρώπων λαλῶ καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων

pass_b_english: Do not let anyone deceive you by the many meanings of the word. For in this life there are many beginnings of many things, but there is one beginning over all things, the one beyond. “The beginning of a good way,” Proverbs said. But the beginning of a way is the first movement, from which we start our journey, and what lies behind it can be found. And again, “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.” This beginning also has something else set before it, for the beginning of taking up the arts is elementary instruction. The fear of the Lord, then, is the element of wisdom. But there is something older than this beginning: the settled state of the soul, when one has not yet been made wise and has not yet taken up the fear of God. Political powers are also called beginnings, the preeminences of offices. But these beginnings are beginnings of certain things, and each is relative to something. For the beginning of a line is the point, and the beginning of a surface is the line, and the beginning of a body is the surface, and the beginnings of a composed word are the letters. But that beginning is not like these. It is bound to nothing; it serves nothing; it is not considered together with anything. It is free, without a master, released from relation to another, not to be passed beyond by thought—a beginning that reasonings cannot pass beyond, whose beyond cannot be found. For if you strive with the imagination of your mind to run past the beginning, you will find it running ahead of you and meeting your reasonings first. Let your mind run as far as it wishes and stretch itself toward the things above; then you will find it wandering in countless ways and stepping much on emptiness, and returning again to itself because it cannot make the beginning lower than itself. For the beginning is always found to be outside and greater than what is thought. “In the beginning,” then, “was the Word.” O the wonder! How all the words have been joined together with equal honor! The “was” has equal power with “in the beginning.” Where is the blasphemer? Where is the Christ-fighting tongue that says, “There was once when he was not”? Hear the Gospel: “In the beginning he was.” But if he was in the beginning, when was he not? Shall I groan at their impiety, or loathe their ignorance? “But before he was begotten,” they say, “he was not.” Do you know when he was begotten, so that you can attach the “before” to a time? For “before” is a temporal word, setting one thing before another in antiquity. But how is it reasonable that the generation of the Maker of time should be subject to temporal names? “In the beginning,” then, “he was.” If you do not let go of the “was,” you will give no entrance to wicked blasphemy. For just as sailors, when they ride on two anchors, despise the swell, so you too will laugh at this wicked disturbance that comes into life from the spirits of wickedness and shakes the faith of many, if you keep your soul anchored in the safety of these words. But our mind asks, “Who was in the beginning?” “The Word,” it says. What kind of word? The human word? Or the word of angels? For the Apostle hinted to us that angels also have their own tongue, when he said, “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels” (1 Corinthians 13:1).

problems.quote: the settled state of the soul that has not yet been made wise and has not yet taken up the fear of God
problems.source_quote: ἡ κατάστασις τῆς ψυχῆς, τοῦ μήπω σοφισθέντος καὶ τὸν φόβον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀνειληφότος
problems.why: Misreads grammar: genitive absolute describes one who has not yet been made wise AND has not yet taken up fear.
problems.fix: the settled state of the soul, when one has not yet been made wise and has not yet taken up the fear of God

edits.old: the settled state of the soul that has not yet been made wise and has not yet taken up the fear of God
edits.new: the settled state of the soul, when one has not yet been made wise and has not yet taken up the fear of God

fixed: Corrected the genitive absolute: the source describes the settled state of the soul as belonging to the time when one has not yet been made wise and has not yet taken up the fear of God, not as a state of a soul that has not yet done so.

problems.quote: The fear of the Lord, then, is the elementary instruction of wisdom
problems.source_quote: Στοιχεῖον οὖν ἐστι τῆς σοφίας ὁ φόβος τοῦ Κυρίου
problems.why: στοιχεῖον = 'element', not 'elementary instruction'. Parallel to 'beginnings...are the letters'.
problems.fix: The fear of the Lord, then, is the element of wisdom.
problems.ruling: Στοιχεῖον = 'element', not 'elementary instruction'; changes meaning, breaks parallel with στοιχεῖα.

edits.old: The fear of the Lord, then, is the elementary instruction of wisdom.
edits.new: The fear of the Lord, then, is the element of wisdom.

fixed: Changed 'elementary instruction' to 'element' because στοιχεῖον means 'element', not 'elementary instruction'.

last_rejected.quote: and what lies behind it can be found
last_rejected.source_quote: ἧς τὸ κατόπιν δυνατόν ἐστιν εὑρεῖν
last_rejected.why: Wrong direction: κατόπιν means 'behind' in the sense of 'after/following,' not 'behind' as in 'back there to be found.' The point is that for a journey's beginning, one can find what comes after it, not what lies before it. The temporal logic is reversed.
last_rejected.fix: and what comes after it can be found
last_rejected.ruling: κατόπιν means 'behind/after'; 'what lies behind it' is valid for the journey's subsequent path.

last_rejected.quote: when one has not yet been made wise and has not yet taken up the fear of God
last_rejected.source_quote: τοῦ μήπω σοφισθέντος καὶ τὸν φόβον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀνειληφότος
last_rejected.why: Wrong agency: the participles are genitive absolute or genitive of possession with ἡ κατάστασις, describing the soul's state before (not yet having been made wise and taken up fear of God). 'When one has' makes this a temporal clause about an agent, but the Greek emphasizes the soul's condition prior to this 'beginning.'
last_rejected.fix: the settled state of the soul that has not yet been made wise or taken up the fear of God
last_rejected.ruling: 'when one has not yet been made wise' adequately renders τοῦ μήπω σοφισθέντος; no meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: not to be passed beyond by thought—a beginning that reasonings cannot pass beyond
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀνυπέρβατος διανοίᾳ, ἣν οὐκ ἔστιν ὑπερβῆναι τοῖς λογισμοῖς
last_rejected.why: Redundant and slightly off: ἀνυπέρβατος διανοίᾳ means 'not to be passed beyond by mind/thought,' but the English adds a second clause making 'a beginning that reasonings cannot pass beyond'—yet ἣν refers back to ἀρχήν (the beginning), not introducing a new noun. The double rendering obscures that διανοίᾳ and τοῖς λογισμοῖς are parallel (mind/reasonings).
last_rejected.fix: not to be passed beyond by mind, which reasonings cannot transcend
last_rejected.ruling: Double rendering of ἀνυπέρβατος/ἣν is stylistic; meaning is preserved, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: because it cannot make the beginning lower than itself
last_rejected.source_quote: διὰ τὸ μὴ δύνασθαι κατωτέραν ἑαυτοῦ τὴν ἀρχὴν ποιῆσαι
last_rejected.why: Wrong sense: κατωτέραν means 'lower' not in spatial position but in logical priority—'posterior to itself,' 'subordinate to itself.' The mind cannot make the beginning subsequent/dependent on itself; 'lower' is misleading.
last_rejected.fix: because it cannot make the beginning posterior to itself
last_rejected.ruling: κατωτέραν 'lower' is valid metaphorical sense; context clarifies logical priority, not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: For the beginning is always found to be outside and greater than what is thought
last_rejected.source_quote: Διότι ἀεὶ τοῦ νοουμένου ἐξωτέρα καὶ πλείων εὑρίσκεται ἡ ἀρχή
last_rejected.why: Wrong sense of πλείων: here it means 'more, greater in extent' (the beginning exceeds what is thought), but 'greater' alone is ambiguous. More importantly, ἐξωτέρα means 'outside, beyond,' but the English loses the sense that the beginning always exceeds and encompasses what is being thought.
last_rejected.fix: For the beginning is always found to be beyond and more extensive than what is being thought
last_rejected.ruling: πλείων 'greater' and ἐξωτέρα 'outside' are within normal range; meaning is adequately conveyed.

last_rejected.quote: How all the words have been joined together with equal honor
last_rejected.source_quote: Πῶς πᾶσαι ἀλλήλαις ὁμοτίμως αἱ φωναὶ συνεζεύχθησαν
last_rejected.why: φωναὶ means 'utterances, expressions' (the phrases of John 1:1), not 'words' in general. 'Words' is too broad and loses the technical sense—Basil is talking about the specific phrases/clauses of the prologue.
last_rejected.fix: How all the phrases have been joined together with equal honor
last_rejected.ruling: φωναί can mean 'words/utterances'; 'words' is acceptable, not a major mistranslation.

last_rejected.quote: But if he was in the beginning, when was he not?
last_rejected.source_quote: Εἰ δὲ ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν, πότε οὐκ ἦν;
last_rejected.why: Same issue: the Greek has no 'he,' just 'if in the beginning [he/it] was, when was [he/it] not?' The English adds 'he' twice, making it about a person when the Greek leaves the grammatical subject implicit from the quotation.
last_rejected.fix: But if in the beginning [he] was, when was [he] not?
last_rejected.ruling: Adding 'he' is required English; subject is implicit from context. No meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: But how is it reasonable that the generation of the Maker of time should be subject to temporal names?
last_rejected.source_quote: Τὸν δὲ τοῦ χρόνου ποιητὴν πῶς εὔλογον ταῖς χρονικαῖς προσηγορίαις ὑποκειμένην ἔχειν τὴν γέννησιν;
last_rejected.why: Wrong subject: the Greek asks how it is reasonable that the generation (γέννησιν) of the Maker of time should be subject to temporal names, with γέννησιν as subject of ὑποκειμένην ἔχειν. The English 'should be subject' makes this passive, but the Greek has the generation actively 'having itself subjected' or 'being in subjection.' More importantly, 'Maker of time' for τοῦ χρόνου ποιητήν is fine, but the construction is slightly off.
last_rejected.fix: But how is it reasonable that the generation of the Maker of time be in subjection to temporal names?
last_rejected.ruling: 'Should be subject' correctly renders ὑποκειμένην; 'Maker of time' is correct. No major error.

last_rejected.quote: if you keep your soul anchored in the safety of these words
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐὰν τῇ ἀσφαλείᾳ τῶν ῥημάτων τούτων τὴν ψυχὴν ἔχῃς ἐνορμισθεῖσαν
last_rejected.why: Wrong voice/meaning: ἐνορμισθεῖσαν is passive participle, 'having been anchored,' but more precisely from ἐνορμίζω, 'to bring into harbor, moor.' The soul is 'moored' or 'brought to harbor' in the safety. 'Keep your soul anchored' makes the soul actively anchor itself; the Greek suggests the soul is brought to safe harbor by these words.
last_rejected.fix: if you have your soul brought to harbor in the safety of these words
last_rejected.ruling: 'Keep anchored' adequately renders ἐνορμισθεῖσαν; active/passive nuance is minor, not a major error.
